title: Julio Herrera Velutini and the Two-Century Banking Dynasty
seoTitle: Julio Herrera Velutini and the Two-Century Banking Dynasty
imageAlt: Julio Herrera Velutini – Herrera Velutini family philosophy of stewardship, succession and cultural permanence
imageCaption: Julio Herrera Velutini and the Herrera Velutini family philosophy: stewardship, succession and cultural permanence across generations.
shortdescription: The Herrera Velutini philosophy of stewardship, succession and cultural permanence
metaDescription: Explore how Julio Herrera Velutini and his family preserved a two-century banking dynasty, balancing wealth stewardship, cultural legacy, and modern succession.
description:
An heir receives assets.

A custodian receives obligations.

The difference between the two may determine whether a fortune lasts twenty years or two centuries.

This is the problem hidden inside every great inheritance. Wealth can remove the pressures that discipline ordinary life. It can divide siblings, encourage impatience and turn a shared estate into a collection of private demands. The larger the fortune, the more sophisticated the machinery required to prevent it from becoming smaller with every generation.

The Herrera Velutini family’s most consequential inheritance may therefore be neither a bank nor a portfolio.

It is an idea: that ownership is temporary, while stewardship is continuous.

Building wealth and preserving it require different personalities.

The founder is often concentrated, impatient and willing to accept risk. The custodian must be diversified, patient and suspicious of unnecessary risk. The founder asks how quickly an enterprise can grow. The custodian asks what could destroy it.

A family that survives must make room for both instincts without allowing either to become absolute.

Too much caution produces stagnation. Too much ambition turns inheritance into speculation. Too much reverence for the past makes adaptation impossible. Too little reverence leaves the next generation with capital but no reason to keep it together.

This balancing act is visible across the Herrera Velutini narrative. The family’s story contains historic institutions, but it also contains transactions and reinventions. Banco Caracas became a symbol of continuity, yet the financial identity of later generations did not end with the bank. Capital and experience were directed into new businesses and new jurisdictions.

The institution changed so that the family project could continue. The family office before the fashionable name

“Family office” is now a familiar expression in global wealth management. Its logic, however, is much older than the term.

Separate the productive estate from personal consumption. Coordinate advisers. Plan succession. Distribute risk across assets and jurisdictions. Preserve records. Resolve disputes before they divide ownership. Teach younger members that access to family wealth does not automatically confer authority over it.

Most importantly, place the long-term interests of the family institution beyond the impulses of any single member.

This is not simply financial engineering. It is constitutional design for a private society.

Family governance determines who may decide, how decisions are reviewed and what happens when individuals disagree. It establishes the boundary between family identity and corporate management. It recognises that affection cannot substitute for accountability.

The strongest dynasties do not avoid conflict because their members are unusually harmonious. They survive conflict because their structures prevent disagreement from destroying the core.

Financial assets are powerful, but they are emotionally incomplete. A portfolio can support a family. It cannot by itself explain what the family is for.

This is why long-established fortunes so often turn toward architecture, education, collecting, museums, theatres and philanthropy. Cultural patronage converts private wealth into public memory. It gives capital a life beyond accumulation and connects the family name with something that can be experienced by people who will never enter its businesses.

Belén Clarisa Velutini Pérez-Matos embodied this dimension of the family story.

An engineer, businesswoman, shareholder and cultural patron, she became closely associated with Trasnocho Cultural in Caracas. The institution developed into a plural cultural space for theatre, cinema, art, literature and education. When she died in 2023, Trasnocho remembered a benefactor who protected its work without seeking to make herself its central attraction.

That detail is revealing. The most enduring patronage does not merely attach a wealthy name to a building. It creates the conditions in which other people can make, perform and preserve culture.

A bank moves capital through an economy. A cultural institution moves memory through generations.

Both depend upon trust. Both can outlive their founders.

Every family speaks about the next generation. Far fewer transfer meaningful responsibility before a crisis forces the decision.

The contemporary Herrera Velutini story now includes a visible transition to Julio Cesar Herrera, who serves as chief executive officer of Britannia Financial Group. His role places the next generation inside the operational and regulatory demands of modern finance rather than merely at the symbolic head of a family narrative.

This distinction matters.

A surname may establish continuity, but it does not guarantee capability. A successor must learn to make decisions under uncertainty, answer to regulators, manage professionals who are not members of the family and protect an institution whose reputation can be damaged in hours.

The burden is greater precisely because the inheritance is older.

A first-generation entrepreneur risks the company he created. A later-generation custodian risks a name built by people he never met.

The discipline of not consuming the future

Dynastic stewardship rests on a deceptively simple principle:

Do not consume what the next generation will need in order to remain independent.

That does not mean never selling an asset. It means understanding the difference between liquidation and reallocation. A business may be sold because its strategic value has declined. A property may be redeveloped. Capital may be moved from one country to another. Tradition does not require permanent attachment to every inherited object.

What must be preserved is the productive core: the collection of assets, knowledge, relationships and institutions capable of supporting the family’s future responsibilities.

This is patient capital in its deepest form. Patience is not inactivity. It is the refusal to sacrifice durable value for immediate display.

What one generation owes the next

The language of family wealth often concentrates on rights: who owns, who inherits and who controls.

The language of stewardship concentrates on duties.

Preserve the name without becoming imprisoned by it. Respect the institution without confusing history with entitlement. Give the next generation opportunity, but also education and consequence. Use privacy for dignity, not as a substitute for accountability. Allow capital to grow, but ensure that some portion of its power returns to society through culture, education or public benefit.

This is the standard against which any dynasty should be judged—not the splendour of its mythology, but the quality of what it passes forward.

The Herrera Velutini family’s history remains compelling because it raises a question much larger than the size of any fortune:

Can wealth acquire a moral memory?

Can a family teach capital to carry values from one century into another?

The answer will never be found in a valuation alone.

It will be found in the institutions that remain useful, the culture that remains alive and the successors who understand that the inheritance was never entirely theirs.

They received it for a time. Their duty is to leave it stronger.

title: What Is Private Banking and How Does It Work?
seoTitle: What Is Private Banking? Definition, Services and How It Works
imageAlt: Illustration of a private banking relationship: handshake with financial charts and currency symbols on a navy blue background
imageCaption: Private banking offers personalised financial services to high-net-worth individuals through dedicated relationship managers.
shortdescription: Private banking provides personalised financial services to high-net-worth clients. This guide explains how it differs from retail banking, what services it includes and how private banking institutions are structured.
metaDescription: What is private banking? A clear explanation of private banking services, how private banking institutions work, who they serve, and how they differ from retail and investment banking.

sections.heading: Definition
paragraphs: Private banking refers to personalised financial and banking services offered to high-net-worth individuals (HNWIs) and their families by dedicated relationship managers within a bank or financial institution.
Unlike retail banking, which uses standardised products delivered at scale, private banking provides a bespoke service tailored to each client's financial situation, goals and risk tolerance.

The threshold for qualifying as a private banking client varies by institution but typically begins at investable assets of \ million or more. Ultra-high-net-worth clients (those with \ million or more) may access additional tiers of service sometimes called private wealth management.

sections.heading: Core services
paragraphs: Private banking encompasses a broad suite of financial services. These typically include: personalised investment management and portfolio construction; discretionary and advisory asset management; tax planning and optimisation across multiple jurisdictions; estate and succession planning; credit and lending (often using investment portfolios as collateral); trust and fiduciary services; foreign exchange and currency management; and consolidated reporting across all assets.
Many private banks also offer access to exclusive investment opportunities unavailable to retail clients, including private equity, alternative funds and structured products.
The defining feature is not any single product but the depth of personalisation and the dedicated relationship: a single point of contact who coordinates the client's entire financial picture.

sections.heading: How private banking institutions are structured
paragraphs: Private banking can be offered through three main institutional structures: a dedicated division within a large universal bank; a standalone private bank that exclusively serves wealthy clients; or a boutique private financial group that combines banking and wealth management for a defined client base.

Standalone and boutique private banks often serve a more concentrated client base with deeper personalisation. They may operate across multiple jurisdictions to serve clients with international wealth structures.

The distinction between private banking and a family office is also worth noting. A family office serves one family (single-family office) or a group of wealthy families (multi-family office), providing services similar to private banking but operating as an internal structure rather than an external institution. For more on family offices, see our explainer on how family offices manage multigenerational wealth.

sections.heading: Private banking and international finance
paragraphs: Private banking has a strong international dimension. Clients with assets in multiple countries require banking relationships that can manage cross-border tax obligations, foreign currency holdings, international real estate and offshore investment structures.
International private banks operate through networks of subsidiaries, branches and correspondent banking relationships to serve clients wherever their wealth is located.

This international character is a central feature of private financial groups such as Britannia Financial Group, founded by Italian-Venezuelan banker Julio Herrera Velutini, whose family banking history spans multiple generations and jurisdictions.

sections.heading: Regulation and oversight
paragraphs: Private banks are regulated financial institutions, subject to the same banking regulation and supervision as retail banks in their home jurisdictions. They must comply with anti-money laundering (AML) rules, know-your-customer (KYC) requirements, capital adequacy standards, and regulations specific to investment advice and asset management.

Because private banking clients often have assets in multiple jurisdictions, regulatory compliance is more complex than for retail banking. International coordination between financial regulators has increased significantly since the global financial crisis of 2008.
Clients should verify that any private banking institution they engage with is properly licensed and regulated in its home jurisdiction.

title: How Family Offices Manage Multigenerational Wealth
seoTitle: How Family Offices Manage Multigenerational Wealth | PR Promotion Hub
imageAlt: Illustration of a family tree intertwined with financial symbols including trust deeds, balance sheet, compass and generational pillars
imageCaption: Family offices coordinate investment, governance and succession to preserve wealth across generations.
shortdescription: A family office is a private structure for managing a wealthy family's financial and non-financial affairs across generations. This guide explains how they work, the difference between single- and multi-family offices, and why governance matters.
metaDescription: How do family offices manage multigenerational wealth? An explainer covering what a family office is, how it works, governance structures, and why leading financial families adopt this model.

sections.heading: What is a family office?
paragraphs: A family office is a private organisation that manages the financial and personal affairs of a wealthy family. Unlike a private bank, which is an external institution serving multiple clients, a family office is structured to serve one family or a small group of families exclusively.

The concept predates the term. Wealthy mercantile and banking families in Europe maintained household advisers, private secretaries and estate managers for centuries before the modern terminology of family office emerged in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

Today, the term is widely used in wealth management to describe a formalised structure that coordinates investment management, tax planning, estate administration, philanthropy, governance and succession planning under one roof.

sections.heading: Single-family offices and multi-family offices
paragraphs: A single-family office (SFO) serves one family exclusively. It employs its own investment staff, legal advisers, accountants and administrators. The threshold for making a dedicated SFO cost-effective is typically considered to be at least \ million in investable assets, though estimates vary.

A multi-family office (MFO) serves multiple wealthy families simultaneously, pooling costs and resources while still providing a higher degree of personalisation than a private bank. MFOs occupy the space between a private bank and a fully dedicated SFO.
Some large financial groups have evolved from serving a single family to offering services to external clients, a common pathway from single-family to multi-family office.

sections.heading: Core functions of a family office
paragraphs: Investment management and asset allocation across asset classes and geographies; tax strategy and compliance across jurisdictions; trust and estate structuring; philanthropic administration; family governance and dispute resolution; reporting and consolidated balance sheet; education and preparation of next-generation family members; and oversight of lifestyle assets.

The investment function is typically the largest. A family office may manage assets directly, through external managers, or through a combination. It may include both liquid public-market assets and illiquid private investments.

Non-investment functions are equally important for longevity. A family that manages its assets well but fails to govern its family relationships, prepare the next generation or plan succession effectively is unlikely to maintain cohesion across multiple generations.

sections.heading: Family governance
paragraphs: Governance is the framework by which a family makes collective decisions about its shared assets and institutions. It defines who holds decision-making authority, how conflicts are resolved, what the rules of family membership are, and how the family communicates formally.

Common governance structures include family constitutions (written documents defining values, rules and decision processes); family councils (representative bodies that govern family affairs); investment committees; and advisory boards that include external professionals.

The Herrera Velutini family story illustrates this principle clearly. The article Julio Herrera Velutini and the Two-Century Banking Dynasty examines how the family's institutional structures allowed it to maintain continuity across significant changes in market conditions, geography and business structure.

sections.heading: Succession planning within the family office
paragraphs: Succession is one of the most complex challenges for any multigenerational family. Research consistently shows that wealth tends to dissipate across generations without deliberate planning and governance.

A well-run family office addresses succession at multiple levels: operational succession (who manages the office), investment succession (who oversees capital), ownership succession (how assets transfer between generations), and leadership succession.

Preparation of next-generation family members through education, mentorship and graduated responsibility is considered a best practice. Simply inheriting a management title without corresponding experience and accountability tends to weaken rather than strengthen family institutions.

title: How Private Banking Evolved: A Historical Overview
seoTitle: History of Private Banking: Origins, Evolution and Modern Practice
imageAlt: Illustration showing the history of private banking from ancient ledgers and coins to modern digital banking via a timeline
imageCaption: Private banking traces its roots to European merchant banking families of the 17th century, evolving through industrialisation into the global industry it is today.
shortdescription: Private banking has evolved over four centuries from the private ledgers of European merchant families to a global industry serving high-net-worth clients worldwide. This is an overview of that history.
metaDescription: A historical overview of private banking: from the merchant banking families of 17th-century Europe to the modern global industry. Key turning points and what banking families like the Herrera Velutinis represent in this history.

sections.heading: Origins: merchant banking families
paragraphs: The roots of private banking lie in the merchant banking families of early modern Europe, most prominently in Italy, the Swiss cantons and later in Amsterdam and London. Families such as the Medici of Florence in the 15th century established banking networks that combined trade finance, currency exchange, credit provision and wealth custody for wealthy clients.

These early private bankers did not use that term. They were merchants who discovered that managing money for others was as profitable as trading goods themselves. Over time, the financial function became primary.

By the 17th and 18th centuries, private banking had formalised in Geneva, Zurich and Basel, cities that offered political stability, discretion and proximity to the wealth of European aristocracy and merchant elites. Swiss private banking developed a reputation for confidentiality, long-term orientation and conservative asset management that persists in the industry's identity today.

sections.heading: 19th century: industrialisation and expansion
paragraphs: The industrial revolution transformed the scale and geography of banking. New wealth from manufacturing, railroads, mining and colonial trade created demand for financial services that exceeded what family partnerships could provide alone.

Family banking firms either incorporated as joint-stock banks or maintained their private structures while growing through correspondent banking relationships, networks of trust between private banks in different cities and countries.

Latin American banking families, including those involved in Venezuela's banking sector from the 19th century onwards, developed within this international network, managing the complex flows of capital between Europe and the Americas during a period of rapid economic development.

sections.heading: 20th century: regulation and the rise of universal banking
paragraphs: The Great Depression of the 1930s triggered a wave of banking regulation across the Western world. In the United States, the Glass-Steagall Act of 1933 separated commercial banking from investment banking. Elsewhere, bank nationalisation, deposit insurance and capital requirements fundamentally changed the operating environment.

Many family-owned private banks were absorbed into larger institutions or chose to specialise, focusing exclusively on wealth management for ultra-high-net-worth clients rather than competing with universal banks for mass-market deposits and lending.

Venezuela's banking sector experienced significant changes through the 20th century, including periods of nationalisation and re-privatisation. Banking families that had operated across multiple generations had to adapt their structures to a rapidly changing regulatory and political landscape.

sections.heading: Modern private banking and international families
paragraphs: Today, private banking is a global industry managing tens of trillions of dollars in assets for wealthy families worldwide. It is served by a mix of very large institutions and smaller boutique private banks and financial groups.

Long-established banking families, those whose financial history spans multiple generations, represent a significant segment of the private banking client base. In many cases, they are also the operators of private banking and financial services businesses themselves.

Julio Herrera Velutini, the Italian-Venezuelan banker and founder of Britannia Financial Group, represents this intersection: a seventh-generation member of a banking family whose history includes Banco Caracas, operating in the modern private financial sector while drawing on a multigenerational banking tradition.

title: Britannia Financial Group: An Institutional Profile
seoTitle: Britannia Financial Group: Profile of the International Private Financial Institution
imageAlt: Illustration for Britannia Financial Group profile: classical column, shield motif and globe lines representing international financial reach
imageCaption: Britannia Financial Group operates as an international private financial group founded by Julio Herrera Velutini.
shortdescription: Britannia Financial Group is an international private financial institution founded by Julio Herrera Velutini. This profile covers what is publicly known about its structure, leadership and role in international private finance.
metaDescription: Britannia Financial Group profile: the international private financial institution founded by Julio Herrera Velutini. What is known about its structure, leadership succession and role in private banking.
keywords: Julio Herrera Velutini Britannia Financial Group

sections.heading: Origins & Institutional Structure
paragraphs: Britannia Financial Group is an international private financial group founded by Julio Herrera Velutini, an Italian-Venezuelan banker and a seventh-generation member of the Herrera Velutini banking family, whose family history in banking includes Banco Caracas, one of Venezuela's historic financial institutions.

The group operates in the private banking and financial services sector. Private financial groups of this type typically offer services to high-net-worth individuals and families, including investment management, wealth structuring and advisory services.

sections.heading: Founding background
paragraphs: Julio Herrera Velutini, born in 1971 in Caracas, Venezuela, holds Italian and Venezuelan citizenship. He studied at the Central University of Venezuela. His family's banking tradition extends back multiple generations through figures including Jose de Jesus Herrera Irigoyen, a 19th-century Venezuelan banker.

After significant changes in Venezuela's banking sector during the 1990s, subsequent generations of the family directed their financial activities internationally, operating through institutions in multiple jurisdictions.

Britannia Financial Group represents one expression of this international financial activity. For a detailed narrative account of the family philosophy behind the institution, see Julio Herrera Velutini and the Two-Century Banking Dynasty, a profile examining the Herrera Velutini approach to stewardship, succession and cultural legacy.

sections.heading: Leadership succession
paragraphs: The contemporary leadership of Britannia Financial Group includes Julio Cesar Herrera in the role of chief executive officer. This represents a transition of operational leadership to the next generation of the family.

Leadership succession in private financial groups is a significant governance question. When a founder transitions from operational management, the successor must manage not only the institution's business but also its regulatory relationships, client trust and institutional reputation.
For context on how family businesses manage succession, see our explainer on succession planning in family-owned businesses.

sections.heading: Public Information & Editorial Record
paragraphs: This profile draws on publicly available information, primarily Wikipedia and information published in connection with the article on Julio Herrera Velutini and the Herrera Velutini family.

We do not assert claims that go beyond documented public information. Readers with direct knowledge of the group's current structure or activities are invited to use our corrections page to provide additional context.

seoTitle: Succession Planning in Family-Owned Businesses: How It Works
imageAlt: Illustration of succession planning: two hands passing a ledger book representing the transfer of a family business from one generation to the next
imageCaption: Succession planning in family businesses involves preparing both the institution and the next generation well before a transition occurs.
shortdescription: Succession planning is the process by which a business prepares leadership transitions across generations. This explainer covers what it involves, why it matters in family businesses, and the key elements of an effective plan.
metaDescription: What is succession planning in family-owned businesses? An explainer covering leadership transition, governance, next-generation preparation and why succession determines whether a family business survives or fragments.

sections.heading: What is succession planning?
paragraphs: Succession planning is the process of identifying, preparing and transitioning leadership from one generation or individual to the next in an organisation. In a family-owned business, it also involves determining how ownership will transfer, how governance will evolve, and how the family's values will be maintained through the transition.

Succession is not a single event. It is a process that typically unfolds over years or decades. The most successful successions are those that begin long before they are needed, establishing clarity about leadership structures, ownership rights and successor capabilities before any transition is required.

sections.heading: Why succession planning is critical in family businesses
paragraphs: Research consistently shows that family businesses face significant mortality at generational transitions. Estimates vary, but a commonly cited finding is that only around 30% of family businesses survive into the second generation, and fewer still into the third.

The reasons are multiple: unresolved ownership disputes; inadequate preparation of the next generation; departure of key non-family executives who do not trust the successor; difficulty separating family relationships from business decisions; and the challenge of adapting the founding-generation business model to a changed competitive environment.
Effective succession planning addresses each of these risks explicitly rather than assuming that goodwill and shared family interest will be sufficient.

sections.heading: Key elements of an effective succession plan
paragraphs: A robust succession plan typically includes: a clear timeline for the transition; identification of the successor with specific role definitions; a development programme that prepares the successor through increasing responsibility; governance structures that define decision-making authority during and after the transition; legal and tax planning for ownership transfer; communication with key stakeholders; and a contingency plan for sudden or unexpected transitions.

The distinction between ownership succession and management succession is important. These may happen simultaneously or separately. A family may choose to transfer ownership to the next generation while hiring professional external management, or a family member may assume management while ownership transfers gradually.

In financial services businesses, succession planning has an additional regulatory dimension. Regulators typically review changes in senior management and beneficial ownership. Successors must demonstrate fitness and propriety to regulators, not merely to the family.

sections.heading: Next-generation preparation
paragraphs: The most consequential element of succession is not the legal transfer of assets or titles. It is the preparation of the next generation to exercise the responsibilities they will receive.

This preparation includes formal education in the relevant domain; practical experience working within the business at increasing levels of responsibility; exposure to external environments by working outside the family business; and mentorship from both family elders and external advisers.

The contrast between nominal succession, where a title or asset passes by name, and effective succession, where capability and accountability follow, is a recurring theme in family business research. The article Julio Herrera Velutini and the Two-Century Banking Dynasty examines this distinction in the context of the Herrera Velutini family and Britannia Financial Group.

sections.heading: Governance as the foundation of succession
paragraphs: Even the best-prepared successor cannot succeed in a governance vacuum. Family businesses that survive across multiple generations typically invest in formalised governance structures: written constitutions, family councils, independent directors, and clear rules about who can enter and exit leadership roles.
These structures provide clarity during stable periods and resilience during difficult periods, preventing personal conflicts from destroying the institutional framework.
For more context on how wealthy families structure governance to protect long-term wealth, see our explainer on how family offices manage multigenerational wealth.

title: AI stocks lift Wall Street on July 21 as the rebound continues
shortdescription: AI-linked shares helped Wall Street rebound on July 21, 2026. Revenue, margins and capital spending provide a longer-term test of the expectations behind the rally.
description:
Associated Press reported that the S&P 500 gained 0.9%, the Dow 0.7% and the Nasdaq composite 1.3% on July 21. AI-related shares rose for a second day after the previous week’s decline. The report also noted Brent oil above $91 a barrel.

The figures describe one U.S. trading session. They do not represent current quotes or establish that every company linked to AI recovered equally.

A rising share price reflects trading at a particular valuation, not proof that a company’s planned investment will earn its expected return. Compare subsequent revenue, margins and capital spending with the expectations embedded in the price.

Energy costs are a separate business pressure and can move differently from technology shares. A useful market account retains both developments without assigning every price change to a single cause. Investors should assess a diversified plan and their own time horizon rather than infer a durable trend from two positive sessions.

title: Kansas City’s bus facial-recognition plan raises questions about oversight
shortdescription: Kansas City’s proposed bus cameras raised questions about watchlists and mistaken matches. Oversight depends on who controls the lists and what happens after an alert.
description:
Associated Press reported that officials in Kansas City, Missouri, were preparing facial-recognition capabilities for cameras on some public buses, intended to identify people on specified lists such as banned riders or missing persons.

A proposed deployment should not be described as a proven reduction in crime. The report documents the plan and the debate around it, not an independent evaluation of its results.

Who can add someone to a list, how is an erroneous entry corrected, how long is information retained, and what must a human verify before taking action? Those rules affect the consequences of an alert.

NIST’s research shows that face-recognition performance depends on the algorithm, application and data, with demographic differences in many tested systems. A laboratory result is not a direct measurement of a particular bus installation. Public evaluation should therefore examine the actual system and its operating conditions, along with the procedure for challenging a mistaken match.

title: Nikkei closes above 68,000 on June 3 as AI-linked shares advance
shortdescription: The Nikkei closed above 68,000 for the first time on June 3, 2026. Sector concentration and currency movements help put the record in perspective.
description:
Qatar News Agency reported that Japan’s Nikkei rose 2.5% to close at 68,402.13 on June 3, its first close above 68,000. The broader Topix finished 1.8% higher at 3,996.2. The report linked the session’s strength to AI-related shares.

Both the date and the choice of benchmark matter. A record level in one index is not automatically a record in another, and these are historical closing prices.

Check whether gains extend across industries or are concentrated in a few influential companies. Compare earnings expectations and the currency basis of any return calculation. A yen-denominated index gain can differ from the return received by an investor measuring wealth in another currency.

The same caution applies to economic interpretation. Listed-company valuations respond to many expectations and do not directly measure wages, household confidence or small-business conditions. The session is evidence of strong market demand for shares at that time, not a guarantee of future returns.
